g.text: MixTransport to Mix Protocol Boundary Flow
01 — Follow one session across the Mix boundary
MIXTRANSPORT / MIX PROTOCOL · ROUTE THROUGH THE TALK
Follow one session across the Mix boundary
A creates session S with B. Either endpoint can open a stream inside that session.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Roadmap: attach Mix · prepare return paths · send forward · send back · recover and dispatch.
02 — Legacy connections and the message API
MIXTRANSPORT / MIX PROTOCOL / CONNECTIONS AND MESSAGES
Legacy connections and the message API
Legacy reply-expecting connections handle one request. MixTransport manages sessions and streams.
with a reference to this connection’s
ExitLayer takes it after the handler returns.
At B: ExitLayer sends the response
Reply returns through Mix; A recovers it.
If the destination is beyond the exit, the exit uses a regular libp2p connection instead of MixExitConnection.
The exit collects that reply using the codec’s response reader.
MixTransport: messages belong to sessions and streams
MixTransport supplies SURBs, retains reply credentials, and dispatches incoming frames.
Mix delivers messages through callbacks instead of an entry connection’s read queue.
Connection objects are local wrappers, not a regular libp2p connection.
03 — The boundary has calls in one direction, callbacks in the other
The boundary has calls in one direction, callbacks in the other
Mix defines the API and callback argument types. MixTransport supplies the receiving handlers.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Register handlers once per transport instance; session and stream dispatch happen inside MixTransport.
04 — Build once, populate the pool, then attach MixTransport
Build once, populate the pool, then attach MixTransport
Storage startup injects a MixProtocol instance into the transport.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
MixProtocol.new does not load the relay list: Storage populates nodePool after construction.
05 — Resolve B, then retain its information for session S
Resolve B, then retain its information for session S
The destination’s physical peer ID and the anonymous session ID serve different purposes.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
B: physical peer ID, endpoint, Mix and libp2p public keys
sendToDestination(B, S, encodedFrame) · internal MixTransport helper
Uses S to look up B’s stored MixPubInfo. The encoded frame already contains sessionId = S.
Intermediate relays still come from the pool.
Without a stored record, the helper calls the peer-ID overload; Mix resolves B from nodePool.
All streams in S share this record. Session teardown removes it.
createReplySurbs calls Mix.createSurb once for each entry, then stores the credentials at A.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
The array index pairs objects during preparation; the arriving packet uses its identifier.
The credential store also records session S and expiry. Credentials are never serialized into the frame.
07 — Connect bootstraps both session state and return capacity
MIXTRANSPORT / MIX PROTOCOL · FIRST FORWARD FRAME
Connect bootstraps both session state and return capacity
A sends five SURBs in one Connect frame; B separates two response SURBs from three supply entries.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
A retains all five credentials. Only the last three entries belong to numbered SURB supply.
08 — Forward delivery: the service selects MixTransport
Forward delivery: the service selects MixTransport
A sends Connect(S); B receives the complete encoded frame through MixDelivery.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Three protocol identifiers, three different jobs
SURBs are inside Connect. Mix does not extract a legacy SURB envelope before this callback.
09 — Reverse delivery: use the supplied return path
Reverse delivery: use the supplied return path
B can send back without A’s physical peer ID, network address or reply credentials.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
ConnectAck uses Connect’s dedicated SURBs. Each send consumes its SURB, even on error.
10 — The reply identifier selects an owner before a session
MIXTRANSPORT / MIX PROTOCOL · RECOVERY AND FALLBACK
The reply identifier selects an owner before a session
MixTransport’s raw-reply callback checks active credentials and remembered retired identifiers.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Handled means “this callback owns the packet”, not “decoding succeeded”. Credentials are not shared.
11 — Local send completion and remote ACK are separate events
MIXTRANSPORT / MIX PROTOCOL · TIMING AND WAITS
Local send completion and remote ACK are separate events
A Mix send waits for local processing and first-hop transmission—not for end-to-end delivery.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Data: remote receive window + retained-send capacity
Ordinary reverse frames: enough SURBs in the session
The send callback is a local seam for tests; in production it forwards to Mix.sendWithSurb.
12 — How reply, session and stream identifiers fit together
How reply, session and stream identifiers fit together
Session IDs, stream IDs and reply identifiers are related locally, but are not interchangeable.
One session: initiator A · recipient B · session S
Omitted: handshake responses, stream opening, ACKs.
Only one of the two redundant Data copies is drawn.
Mix owns routing and cryptography. MixTransport owns sessions, streams, supply and credential lifetime.
In both modes, replies return via SURBs. At A, recovered bytes enter the requesting connection’s incoming queue.
